label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Subject: The building — you need to call me**

Denis,

I tried to write this email maybe ten times since Thursday. Each time it came out half in French and half in words I don't want your wife to read. So I'm going slow, and in English, so there is no confusion about what I mean.

I know about the listing. I know about the agent, and I know the price, 1,150,000$. I found it myself on Centris, after.

But that's not how I learned. On Thursday at 6 in the morning I was in the back shaping the baguettes like every morning for 31 years, and a man with a camera walked into my shop. He said he was from the agency, here to take pictures for the sale. He said Mr. Denis told him I was okay with it.

Okay with it. Denis, I did not even know.

I stood there with dough on my hands in front of a stranger who knew more about my own building than I did. Karine had to take me outside to calm me down. I am 57 years old and my employee had to calm me down like a child in front of the ovens. I don't think I have been so humiliated in my life.

So yes, I am furious. I'm not going to pretend I'm not, because you would know I'm lying.

What hurts most is not even the sale. It's the way. After maman's funeral you called me and said "no rush, we decide together." I remember the words exactly because they made me feel better that day. Together. Then you put our father's building on the market without one phone call, and you let an agent's photographer be the one to tell me. If you had called and said "I want to sell, I need the money, let's talk," I would have been upset, but I would have understood. We would have talked like brothers. Instead you sent a stranger. I'm sorry, Denis, but that is the act of a coward, and I know you are not a coward, so I don't understand.

I want to remind you of some things, because I think from Calgary maybe they look small.

Papa bought that building in 1979. The bakery downstairs, the two apartments upstairs. I have been in that bakery for 31 years. Since the estate was settled in August, the building is half yours and half mine. I'm not asking for more than my half. But I'm also not a tenant who just showed up.

I pay 2,400$ a month to the estate and I have never been late once. Not one month. In 2019, when the roof was finished, I paid for the new one myself, 38,000$, because it had to be done and I didn't want to bother maman with it. I never asked anybody to pay me back. I'm not saying this to throw it in your face. I'm saying it because I took care of that building like it was going to stay in the family. I thought that was the plan.

I also want you to remember what I told you in September on the phone. I want to buy your half. The caisse pre-approved me for 410,000$. I know that's not the same number as the agent's price, but that's the agent's price, not a fact, and it's exactly the kind of thing we can sit down and work out. Maybe the roof counts for something. Maybe there's another way, payments over time, I don't know. But you didn't even give me the chance to talk about it. You went straight to the market like my offer was nothing.

I know what you think. You think I'm being sentimental, that I'm attached to the old walls and the smell of bread and papa's memory, and that this is business. Okay. Let's talk business.

I have 6 employees. Some of them have been with me more than ten years. I have 31 years of clients, people who come every morning, people whose kids I saw grow up and who now bring their own kids. My lease finishes on April 30, 2027. You know who buys a building like ours on Saint-Hubert at that price. A developer. Either he tears it down for condos, or he keeps it and doubles my rent the day the lease ends. I can't survive double rent. Nobody in this business can. So it's not only about feelings. It's my living, it's six other people's living, and it's a business our father started in that building. I'm not sentimental. I'm doing the math, and the math says the shop dies.

And yes, there's the sentimental part too, I won't hide it. Do you remember the little room in the back, the one with the flour sacks? Papa let you sleep there when we were kids. You loved it. You used to make a bed in the sacks and say it was the best place in the whole house. You came out white like a ghost and maman would get mad and papa would laugh. That room is still there, Denis. I walk past it every morning. I can't believe the same boy who slept in the flour is now selling it to a stranger without telling me.

So here is what I'm asking.

Take the building off the market this week. If you really can't do that, then at minimum give me the first right to buy your half before anybody else, in writing, so I have a real chance. That's not a big thing to ask. That's what family does. That's what "we decide together" means.

And I want your answer by phone, from you. Not a text, and not a message from your wife. I love her, and I know she reads English better than you, and I'm grateful she will help you with this letter. But this is between you and me. It's between papa's two sons. You owe me a phone call, at least that.

I want to be very clear about one more thing, because I'm angry and I don't want it to come out wrong. I don't hate you. I'm hurt, I'm insulted, and right now I'm very angry with you. But you are my brother, and since maman is gone, you are the only one left who remembers that house and that bakery the way I do. I don't want to lose my building, and I really don't want to lose my brother over it. I think papa would be ashamed to see us like this, and I think he would be most ashamed of how it happened.

We can fix this. But you have to call me.

Call me this week.

Your brother
